extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science, practicing scientists, and graduate students interested in the nature of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and concepts for assessing scientific paradigms and paradigm change: what counts as a scientific problem, what solutions are legitimate, and how observation, instruments, and standards shift with revolutions in science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content differences between paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive paradigms tell us different things about the population of the universe and about that population’s behavior (e.g., existence of subatomic particles, materiality of light, conservation of heat or energy). These are the substantive differences between successive paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a theory or paradigm, examine the substantive claims it makes about what entities exist and how they behave. Examples: disputes about particles vs. waves, conservation laws. Scoring note: substantive novelty or change in ontology is a central axis of paradigm change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms as sources of methods, problem-fields, and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigms are directed not only to nature but also back upon the science that produced them; they are the source of the methods, problem-field, and standards of solution accepted by any mature scientific community at any given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a paradigm by the methods it legitimates, the problems it defines as central, and the standards it uses to judge solutions. Example: the corpuscular paradigm directed attention to collisions and contact forces. Anti-pattern: evaluating a paradigm only by its empirical fit while ignoring the methodological and problem-setting roles it plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of problems is paradigm-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Some old problems may be relegated to another science or declared entirely 'unscientific.' Others that were previously non-existent or trivial may, with a new paradigm, become the very archetypes of significant scientific achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which problems a paradigm treats as legitimate or irrelevant. When peer-reviewing work, consider whether the research addresses problems that are recognized as legitimate within its paradigm and whether a paradigm shift might reclassify its significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards that distinguish scientific solutions from non-scientific
rubrics_metrics.description: As the problems change, so, often, does the standard that distinguishes a real scientific solution from a mere metaphysical speculation, word game, or mathematical play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether proposed solutions meet the paradigm-specific standards (explanatory power, empirical adequacy, coherence with accepted methods). Note that what counts as a scientific solution can change with the paradigm; apply the standards current to the community or explicitly justify departures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation-by-hindsight is inadequate for guiding research
rubrics_metrics.description: Though an out-of-date theory can always be viewed as a special case of its up-to-date successor, the transformation is one that can be undertaken only with the advantages of hindsight... that restatement would have utility, but it could not suffice for the guidance of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid retrofitting historical or rival theories into the language of the current paradigm as a basis for claiming they were 'essentially correct.' For evaluation, prioritize whether a theory, as understood within its own historical/paradigmatic context, provided guiding problems and methods rather than only whether it can be recast as a limiting case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms must be productive (generate problems and solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The corpuscular paradigm bred both a new problem (e.g., collisions) and a large part of that problem’s solution; paradigms are often productive in suggesting new problems and fruitful lines of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a paradigm’s scientific fruitfulness by whether it opens new problem-fields and research techniques that lead to successful results (e.g., Newton embedding prior results in laws). In peer review, consider the research program’s ability to generate testable questions and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and progress are not necessarily cumulative
rubrics_metrics.description: The case for cumulative development of science’s problems and standards is hard to make. Changes in standards are not necessarily a raising or lowering but a change demanded by the adoption of a new paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume newer paradigms are simply better by some external metric. When evaluating claims of progress, be explicit about the criteria used; recognize that different paradigms embed different standards and that external value judgments may be required to compare them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm debates cannot be resolved solely by normal-science criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent that two scientific schools disagree about what is a problem and what is a solution, they will inevitably talk through each other... recourse to external criteria makes paradigm debates revolutionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In adjudicating disputes between competing paradigms, acknowledge the limits of normal-science arguments. Be prepared to invoke extra-scientific or meta-scientific criteria (values, priorities, broader theoretical virtues) if necessary, and make these explicit in reviews or comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation is theory-laden (perception depends on prior training)
rubrics_metrics.description: What a man sees depends both upon what he looks at and also upon what his previous visual-conceptual experience has taught him to see (illustrated by gestalt experiments, inverting-lens experiments, anomalous playing-card experiments, and historical examples such as Lavoisier seeing oxygen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating empirical claims, account for the role of background theory and training in shaping observations. Look for behavioral/experimental indicators that a new category or phenomenon is being reliably perceived (e.g., reproducibility, changes in instrument practice), rather than relying solely on testimonial claims of 'seeing' something new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for perceptual/paradigmatic shifts is indirect and behavioral
rubrics_metrics.description: With scientific observation the scientist can have no recourse above or beyond what he sees with his eyes and instruments; if perceptual switches accompany paradigm changes, we may not expect scientists to attest to them directly. We must look for indirect and behavioral evidence that the scientist with a new paradigm sees differently from before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical or contemporary evaluation, seek indirect evidence of paradigm change: shifts in instrumentation, criteria for acceptable data, new experimental practices, new categories applied to familiar phenomena, and downstream research outputs. Explicit first-person testimony about 'seeing differently' is generally not available or decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruments and prototypes shape what is seen and counted as data
rubrics_metrics.description: Led by a new paradigm, scientists adopt new instruments and look in new places; the assimilation of a paradigm changes what instruments reveal and which features become salient (e.g., Herschel's telescope, Hauksbee's apparatus, Leyden jar reinterpreted as condenser).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how instrumentation and standard experimental setups have changed under a paradigm. Consider whether observed phenomena become detectable or reinterpretable only with new instruments or prototypes; this can be evidence of genuine paradigmatic transformation rather than mere reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and classification are paradigm-conditioned
rubrics_metrics.description: A celestial body that had been observed off and on for almost a century was seen differently after 1781 because it could no longer be fitted to the perceptual categories (star or comet) provided by the previous paradigm (example: Uranus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of discovery or reclassification in light of the classificatory schemes operative in the relevant community. Determine whether a claimed 'new' phenomenon reflects a genuine change in classification criteria rather than simple improvement in detection.
